roots.name: MOS 6510 CPU, 40-pin DIP
roots.description: 8-bit NMOS microprocessor at U7 of the C64 mainboard, clocked at 1.022727 MHz NTSC (0.985248 MHz PAL). It is the 6502 core plus an 8-bit I/O port on pins 9/10 (address 0000 data-direction, 0001 output latch). The MOS/CSG datasheet calls it 'HMOS, silicon gate, depletion load technology' - i.e. an N-channel silicon-gate double-polysilicon process with depletion-mode load devices, roughly a 2 um minimum feature. Fabbed in-house by MOS Technology (later Commodore Semiconductor Group) at 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown, Pennsylvania.

facts.label: Process
facts.value: NMOS silicon gate, double poly, depletion load (datasheet says 'HMOS')

places: Norristown, Pennsylvania, USA (MOS Technology / CSG fab)
roots.note: MOS called its fast N-channel process 'HMOS'; here it means a NMOS process with an ion-implanted polysilicon gate, not the HMOS of later MOS parts. The exact minimum linewidth of the Norristown 6510 (2 um vs 3 um) is not published; treat the 2 um figure as medium confidence.

children.name: Polished 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
children.description: The starting substrate for the die: a 4-inch (100 mm) Czochralski-grown, boron-doped p-type silicon wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished mirror finish on one face, 300-350 um thick, with a primary flat and a small secondary orientation flat.

facts.label: Diameter
facts.value: 100 mm (4 inch) - 125 mm was not standard until ~1986

children.note: P-type (100) CZ was the standard NMOS logic substrate through the 1980s; n-type epitaxial and (111) were alternatives.

children.name: 9N-11N electronic-grade polysilicon
children.description: Chunky polycrystalline silicon chunks loaded into the Czochralski crystal puller. Made by the Siemens process: high-purity trichlorosilane is reduced with pure hydrogen over electrically heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C, depositing polycrystalline silicon on the hot wires until a rod ~150-250 mm diameter and about 1 m long is grown.

children.name: Siemens wire-heated deposition reactor
children.description: A vertical bell-jar or can reactor holding 40-80 U-shaped silicon filaments wound from vapor-grown poly. A few hundred amps of DC is passed through the filaments to hold them at ~1150 C while SiHCl3 vapour decomposes on them. These reactors were the standard ultra-purity route until the late 1980s.

children.name: Trichlorosilane (SiHCl3), 9N-11N
children.description: The intermediate that carries silicon from cheap metallurgical-grade metal to electronics grade. Made by passing dry HCl over crushed metallurgical silicon at 250-350 C in a fluidised or bubbling bed: Si + 3 HCl -> SiHCl3 + H2. Rectified by fractional distillation to a boiling point of 31.8 C until metal, B and P contaminants are below 1 ppb.

children.name: Hydrogen chloride from salt and chlorine
children.description: Dry HCl gas made by chlorinating hydrogen over a bed of rock salt, or by burning hydrogen in chlorine, then condensing and drying it with concentrated sulfuric acid. The chlorine itself comes from electrolysis of brine.

children.name: Chlor-alkali brine electrolysis
children.description: Salt dissolved in water electrolyzed in a membrane or mercury cell at 3-4 V to make chlorine and hydrogen; the hydrogen is what reacts with the salt to make HCl and what reduces the trichlorosilane.

children.name: Rock salt for the chlor-alkali cell
children.description: Halite mined by room-and-pillar or solution mining in the Michigan basin, Louisiana's Salt Dome, the Cheshire salt field (which is why a US chlor-alkali industry sat on top of salt), and the Zechstein basin of northern Germany. Brine is made by pumping water into the salt and pumping out saturated brine.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
children.description: Rough grey lumps of silicon produced in a submerged arc furnace from quartz and petroleum coke at 1900-2200 C. This is the ore-like starting point: roughly 300 kg of 98% silicon per 6510-class wafer batch. Boron and phosphorus ride along at hundreds of ppm and must be removed later.

children.name: Submerged arc furnace, 20-40 MVA
children.description: A refractory-lined steel shell 10-12 m deep with three graphite electrodes lowered into a charge of quartz lump, petroleum coke and wood chips. Electric current (200-400 kA at 40-70 V) maintains an arc that melts the charge in the 'submerged zone' at 1900-2200 C, tapping grey metallic silicon out of the bottom every 1-2 hours. Up to 4 t/day in a modern furnace; a 1982-era unit made a few hundred tonnes per year.
children.note: Metallurgical silicon was traded globally; US and European silicon metal plants in 1982 were mainly in West Virginia, Quebec and the German Ruhr.

children.name: Quartz (SiO2) lump for the arc furnace
children.description: High-purity quartz, ideally with under 200 ppm aluminium and iron, crushed to 5-30 mm. Because aluminium in the metal feeds straight through to every device, silicon makers specify vein quartz or purified lump.

children.name: Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2
children.description: The geologic end of the whole tree. Sand washed from a high-purity quartzite or sandstone deposit, then purified for semiconductor use by acid leaching (HF + HNO3 to strip Al and Fe) and by chlorination, yielding quartz that can be melted into crucibles or reacted with HCl.
children.note: Mined quartz of this quality is found only in a handful of districts; Spruce Pine NC is the classic North American source.

children.name: Pegmatite / quartzite ore, mined and crushed
children.description: The actual dig: a hard-rock pegmatite or high-purity quartzite vein, blasted and jaw-crushed, then screened and hand-sorted to 5-30 mm lump for the arc furnace. Only a fraction of a deposit is white enough to be metallurgical-grade.

children.name: Feldspar and mica gangue, hand-picked away
children.description: The pegmatite that hosts the quartz veins contains albite/K-feldspar and muscovite/BIOTite. Alumina in feldspar is the enemy - it survives all the way to the aluminium metallization - so the lump is sorted by hand and by hydrofluoric-acid washing before it is even shipped.
children.note: Biotite in particular carries a lot of iron and is a classic contaminant marker.

children.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
children.description: Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible rather than the arc furnace is crushed to sand, then hot-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 to dissolve surface aluminium and iron, chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip B, P, As and alkali metals, and finally annealed in vacuum. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.
places: Spruce Pine, NC (Unimin, Quartz Corp, GE Quartz)

children.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
children.description: HF is made by treating finely ground fluorspar (CaF2) with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead/cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. It attacks glass and is the standard etchant for thermal oxide; huge quantities of it went through the same silicon supply chain.

facts.label: Consumption
facts.value: ~1 kg HF per wafer for oxide steps, reused several times

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
children.description: Acid-grade fluorspar mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits, beneficiated by flotation to 97%+ purity. Large deposits in Mexico (San Luis Potosi), South Africa (Plettenberg Bay) and China. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching, no quartz purification and no cleaning chemistry.
children.note: Mid-1980s concern: the 1986 Chernobyl release was fluorine (not fluorspar), but fluorspar supply concentration in Mexico is genuine.

children.name: Sulfuric acid from sulfur, from pyrite or natural gas
children.description: Contact-process sulfuric acid: sulfur (mined as Frasch-free elemental sulfur, or roasted from pyrite ore) is burned and catalytically oxidised over V2O5 to SO3, absorbed in 98% H2SO4. Used both for HF manufacture and for the Piranha clean.

children.name: Petroleum coke as the carbon reductant
children.description: Needle coke or calcined petroleum coke from a petroleum coke calciner, used as both reductant and fuel in the arc furnace. Also the ancestor of the graphite electrodes and of the epoxy resin later on in the package.

children.name: Delayed coking and calcination of petroleum coke
children.description: Vacuum residue from crude oil distillation is heated in a battery of delayed-coking heaters to 500 C and held in a large coking drum for 12-24 hours, then the green coke is calcined in a rotary kiln at 1200-1350 C to drive off volatiles and leave 0.5-2% sulphur needle coke. In the silicon industry a blend of petroleum coke and anthracite coal is used instead.
inputs: vacuum residue from crude oil distillation

children.name: Sour crude residue, vacuum distilled
children.description: Heavy Venezuelan or Middle East crude sent to a vacuum tower at 350-400 C / 30-50 mmHg; the bottoms, a dense black pitch of asphaltenes and metal porphyrins, are the feed for coke. Vanadium and nickel concentrate in this residue, so coke made from it carries trace vanadium that the silicon plant has to tolerate.

children.name: Anthracite coal as a coke substitute
children.description: The other traditional reductant for the submerged arc furnace, mined from the hard coal fields of Pennsylvania, Wales and Shanxi. Lower carbon, higher ash and higher iron than petroleum coke, so it was used as a blend component.

children.name: Czochralski growth of the boron-doped ingot
children.description: The puller melts polysilicon chunks in a fused quartz crucible at ~1420 C in a flowing helium or argon atmosphere, dips a seed crystal, and rotates and slowly withdraws it while a raw boule ~100 mm across and 1-1.5 m long grows. Boron trichloride or diborane is dosed into the melt to set the 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity. The constant rotation and the thermal gradient grow a dislocation-free, uniform cross-section with a slight oxygen precipitate peak near the seed end.
children.note: No N-type epitaxy was needed for NMOS: the transistor bodies are p+ islands diffused into the p-type substrate. Epitaxial growth in this period was done in an ATCP (Applied Technology) vertical radiant-heated reactor.

children.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
children.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm ID, holding several kilos of molten silicon and dipping into it several cm at 1420 C. It is itself grown from quartz sand in a flame-fusion electric furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel, annealed slowly to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out. Crucibles were the dominant silicon-metal loss source and were scrapped after a handful of pulls.

children.name: Quartz sand melted into crucible glass
children.description: High-purity quartz sand, acid-leached to remove aluminium and iron, is melted in a flame/arc furnace around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C into a clear annealed vitreous silica blank. Graphite is then burnt off in air at 800-1000 C.

children.name: Seed crystal for CZ pulling
children.description: A short (100 mm) (100)-oriented sliver cut from a previous ingot, used to set the orientation and defect-free growth of the new boule.

children.name: Float zone alternative (silicon for other parts, not the 6510)
children.description: In float-zone growth a poly rod is converted to monocrystal by dragging a molten silicon zone down it in an inert atmosphere, touching no crucible at all. Yield is higher and oxygen is lower, but the crystals were narrow (<30 mm) and slow, so FZ in 1982 was for power rectifiers and some bipolar parts, not CPU wafers.
children.note: Included because it is the other way to grow a boule, and it explains why FZ silicon appears in some C64-era discrete rectifiers.

children.name: Helium as the CZ growth atmosphere
children.description: High-purity helium (6N) bled over the melt to carry off the intense blackbody heat and to sweep volatile boron compounds away. Argon or a helium/argon mix was a cheaper alternative and produced more oxygen precipitation.

children.name: Ingot slicing: ID or OD saw + laser scribe
children.description: The boule is ground round, a sapphire-orientation-reference crystal is used to find the (100) direction, and the wafer flats are laser-scribed (ruby or Nd:YAG) before cutting. Slicing was by OD saw (blade up to 2.2 m diameter, rotating at 2000 rpm, ~0.30 mm kerf) or, on more advanced 1982 machines, by ID saw (blade inside the crystal, ~0.25 mm kerf). The result is ~0.7 mm wafers, far too warped and marked to print on.

children.name: Diamond-impregnated saw blade
children.description: A thin steel or resin-bonded wheel whose rim carries a diamond grit. Slicing 100 mm silicon at 2-3 wafers a minute relies on that grit: natural or synthetic industrial diamond, 20-40 um for a roughing cut and 3-5 um for the finish cut. Resin-bonded blades were introduced in the mid 1970s and gave a thinner kerf and less bow than the metal bond.

facts.label: Blade
facts.value: resin-bonded, OD up to 2.2 m; ID blades inside the boule

children.name: Industrial diamond from graphite
children.description: Saw-grade industrial diamond in 1982 was mostly synthetic: graphite pressed and sintered into a diamond-metal catalyst (Fe, Co, Ni) at 5-6 GPa and 1300-1600 C in a belt press. Natural diamond - the harder, scarcer gem and industrial grade - came from kimberlite pipes in South Africa, Botswana and Russia.

facts.label: Natural source
facts.value: kimberlite pipe, Gaborone and Kimberley, South Africa

places: Element Six (De Beers), UK; Sumitomo Electric, Japan

children.name: Double-sided lapping
children.description: Saw-cut wafers are lapped on a rotating cast-iron plate against a conditioning plate using a slurry of colloidal silica or alumina in water, taking them to ~300 um with a mirror surface but still several micrometres of total thickness variation across the wafer.

children.name: Wet chemical polish (not CMP)
children.description: 1982 practice: the wafer was chemically polished in hot alkaline or acidic peroxide solution - for example hot dilute NaOH/H2O2, or HNO3/HF/acetic - which removed ~10 um of damage layer and left an atomically flat surface. Chemical-mechanical polishing with a soft pad and slurry did not reach volume production until the late 1980s.
children.note: Difference from today: a modern wafer goes through CMP in a rotary single-wafer polisher; in 1982 this step was purely chemical.

children.name: Edge profiling / edge chamfer
children.description: The wafer rim was rounded by a brief hot KOH or NH4OH etch, removing the razor edge so later photoresist could not build up and so the wafer would not chip in handling.

children.name: Pre-diffusion wafer clean: Piranha and RCA SC-1
children.description: Every wafer entering the furnace was cleaned. The workhorse step was Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C, boiling off organics and metal), followed by RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O 1:1:5 at 75-80 C) and SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), then a megasonic rinse in deionized water and a short HF dip to strip native oxide. Megasonic (1.6 MHz sonic) cleaners and particle-count-filtered N2 blow-off were standard.

children.name: Ultrapure deionized process water
children.description: City water passed through sand, activated carbon, cation and anion exchange resins, a 1.5 micron filter and finally UV sterilization to reach 10-18 Mohm-cm and under 100 ppt dissolved solids. Every C64 die consumed thousands of litres of this water across its ~50 dip and rinse steps.

children.name: Photomask set, ~10 levels
children.description: The 6510 pattern was drawn as polygons on a Calma/Computervision layout system, converted through a mask database to mask data, and cut into 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates for a 100 mm wafer. Nine or ten mask levels: n+ S/D, field, contact, poly, second contact, metal, passivation/pad, plus alignment and test structures. For a device this small the fab used 1:1 masks with contact or proximity printing; 10x steppers were brand new in 1982.

facts.label: Mask type
facts.value: 1:1, chrome on soda-lime glass or quartz, 5x7 inch

children.note: The exact level count and whether any mask was a reticle is not published for the Norristown 6510. Commodore did own mask-making capability, but I have not verified the West Hills facility mentioned in some accounts.

children.name: Chrome-on-glass photomask plate
children.description: A 5x7 inch plate of 1 mm soda-lime glass or fused quartz coated with ~100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, then exposed and developed in positive photoresist, then the exposed chromium etched away in hot sulfuric-perchromate or perchloric acid, washed, inspected, and defect-repaired.

children.name: Sputter target of chromium
children.description: 99.5% pure chromium cathode, vacuum-melted and rolled, sputtered with argon at ~1-2 kW onto the rotating plate inside a DC magnetron chamber. Chromium's high opacity in the deep-UV and its resistance to wet cleaning made it the universal mask absorber from the 1960s to the present.
places: mask shops in California and Taiwan

children.name: Mask plate glass from melted quartz sand
children.description: Soda-lime float glass (most 1982 1:1 masks) or fused silica, melted from batched sand plus soda ash and lime in a continuous tank furnace and drawn into 1 mm plate, then annealed.

children.name: Pattern generator driving a mask exposure
children.description: In 1982 most masks of this size were made by a numerically controlled pattern generator that flashed a xenon-mercury lamp through an aperture and shutter wheel in a raster of rectangles into a camera-reduction stage, or by a 1:1 mask writer that exposed a blank plate directly. Electron-beam mask writers (EBG, Santa Clara) existed but at roughly US$1-2 million were not typical in a small internal device fab.
children.note: Whether Norristown used an in-house plotter, a purchased mask from an outside mask shop, or a mix is not documented in public sources.

children.name: Photoresist for mask making
children.description: Positive resists of the era: Shipley AZ-1350 and AZ-1354 (which also served as the wafer resist for most process levels), Kodak KMR-8105, and Fuji HiP resist. Resist spun at ~3000 rpm to 0.5-1.5 um, soft-baked at 90-100 C, exposed in N2, developed in dilute alkaline developer.
places: Rohm and Haas, Philadelphia; Fuji Film, Japan; Hitachi, Japan
children.note: Shipley (Rohm and Haas) was headquartered in Philadelphia, 30 km from the Norristown fab, as was the later Rohm and Haas mask-resist business - a real regional supply chain.

children.name: Mask inspection and defect repair
children.description: Masks were checked on a Zeiss or KLA comparison mask inspection tool against the design database, printing defect-free chrome checkouts. Opaque defects on clear areas were repaired with a fine gallium or indium needle or by lifting the film and re-exposing; clear defects in a chrome line were patched with deposited carbon. Pellicles (1-2 um Mylar membranes mounted in a frame) protected final production masks from dust; Commodore bought chips on wafers or in flatpacks and cut them at assembly instead, but many C64-era NORISTOWN parts were shipped in this way.
children.note: Pellicles were in general use by 1982 but were less common for 1:1 contact printing, where the mask still touched the wafer.

children.name: The 10x stepper arriving at the end of the period
children.description: Reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire, and later ASML) that printed a 10x-reduced reticle with a +-0.2-0.3 um overlay and broke the industry below the 1 um limit. By 1982 a 1:1 contact printer could just barely hold a 2 um line, so a 2 um 6510 was still printable 1:1; the steppers were arriving for the next generation, not for this part. Canon FPA-series 10x machines were among the first installed.
children.note: Named machines are illustrative of the period rather than confirmed as sitting in Norristown.

children.name: 2 um NMOS front end: the layer stack
children.description: A silicon-gate, double-polysilicon NMOS process flow on p-type (100) CZ silicon: heavily doped n+ source/drain first, LOCOS field oxide, heavily n-doped polysilicon gate, self-aligned arsenic source/drain, contact cuts, aluminium metallization, then phosphosilicate glass plus a plasma nitride seal. Ten mask levels, ~50 major process steps, roughly 6-8 weeks of fab cycle time.

facts.label: Layers
facts.value: single aluminium level, single poly gate + poly load resistor

children.note: Layer thicknesses for the specific 6510 are reconstructed from period NMOS design rules, not from a published process manual. There was exactly ONE metal layer - no aluminium barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP, no dual damascene.

children.name: 1. n+ source/dank pre-diffusion
children.description: A thermal phosphorus diffusion: the wafer is coated with a phosphosilicate glass (PSG) doped by PH3 or by a PBN (pyrolytic boron nitride) solid phosphorus source, then held at 900-950 C for 30-60 minutes to push phosphorus about 0.5-1 um into the silicon. The result is a heavily doped (10^20 cm^-3) n+ region that will become the bit-line/tap contact landing areas and the bases of the load and driver devices.
children.note: Some 1982 fabs used an arsenic implant instead of phosphorus diffusion; Norristown is documented only as an NMOS shop, not at this level of detail.

children.name: 2. LOCOS field oxide
children.description: The active-area mask is defined in photoresist over the grown oxide, and field oxide grown by two-step thermal oxidation: a dry O2 pass at ~1000 C to lay down the thin masking oxide, then steam at the same temperature for ~2 hours to reach 6000-8000 A of field oxide. Field oxide was the isolation, the mask for the self-aligned source/drain implant, and the thickest feature on the die.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: dry O2 then wet H2/O2, 1000-1100 C

facts.label: Bird's beak
facts.value: ~1-2 um lateral encroachment - the reason a field-gate design was attractive

children.note: LOCOS was still the isolation scheme in 1982; trench isolation was a few years away.

children.name: 4. Poly gate oxidation (the real '3.5 V' gate dielectric)
children.description: After the undoped polysilicon is patterned, the whole wafer is re-oxidised: the bare silicon is left capped by the 400 A screen oxide, while the poly itself grows its own oxide. Dry O2 at 1000-1100 C for 30-90 minutes grows ~350-450 A of silicon dioxide on the poly, converting it into a depletion-mode MOSFET with the same gate dielectric as the silicon. This is why 'the gate oxide was grown in an oxygen furnace' is literally true of silicon-gate NMOS - but on the poly, not on the channel.

facts.label: Thickness
facts.value: 350-450 A (~800 A grown to allow for later poly oxidation)

children.name: 3. Deposition and doping of the polysilicon
children.description: Polysilicon was deposited by low-pressure chemical vapour deposition in a heated-wall tube furnace from silane (SiH4) at 800-850 C or from dichlorosilane (SiH2Cl2) at ~1000 C, giving 4000-8000 A of polycrystalline film. For gates it was deposited heavily n-doped in the same step by adding phosphine to the silane flow. Undoped poly, or lightly doped poly, was also deposited in the same furnace as the load resistors and as the depletion-mode loads the 6510 datasheet describes.
children.note: Dichlorosilane was cheaper per deposited atom than silane and preferred for thick films, but carried chlorine that required a careful post-deposition clean.

children.name: 5. Self-aligned source/drain implant
children.description: With the poly gate and field oxide standing up, the wafer is ion-implanted with arsenic (or phosphorus) at 50-150 keV. The gate poly and the field oxide act as their own masks, so the source and drain edges are formed automatically under the poly edges with no alignment tolerance at all. The implanted arsenic is then annealed at 1000-1100 C in dry O2 or N2, which also drives it under the gate edge and repairs implant damage.

facts.label: Why it matters
facts.value: self-alignment is what made 2 um silicon-gate NMOS practical in a small fab

children.name: 6. Contact cut and aluminium metallization
children.description: Contact windows are cut in the field oxide with an HF dip masked by photoresist (silicon dioxide etches fast in HF), then the wafer is coated by vacuum evaporation or DC sputtering with 1-2 um of aluminium containing 0.5-1% silicon to stop aluminium spikes punching through thin junctions. The aluminium is patterned by a hot phosphoric-acid etch (H3PO4:HNO3:acetic acid/water at ~50-80 C) or, from the late 1970s, by a CF4/O2 plasma in a barrel etcher.
children.note: Difference from today: no refractory barrier, no tungsten plug, no CMP-defined metal lines, and a single aluminium layer - the die simply had no room for more.

children.name: 7. Passivation and pad opening
children.description: The aluminium is sealed under a phosphosilicate glass overcoat grown by CVD from TEOS and phosphine at 700-800 C, and in 1982-84 plants increasingly by plasma-enhanced CVD silicon nitride (~700 C, SiH4/NH3 or SiCl4/NH3 in a low-frequency glow discharge). Pad windows are opened with a hot phosphoric acid etch of the nitride followed by a buffered HF dip.
children.note: Whether the 6510 die carried nitride passivation or only PSG is not publicly documented; nitride passivation at a small internal fab in 1982 is plausible but not certain.

children.name: Positive photoresist: spin, soft-bake, expose, develop
children.description: Wafer coated on a spinner (2000-4000 rpm) to 1-2 um of AZ-1350, dried 90-100 C for 20-30 min on a hot plate, aligned to the mask in a Coburn 2400 contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2 optical proximity aligner, exposed through the chrome plate, then spray-developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide. Between every step: megasonic clean, dilute H2SO4:H2O2, and a hard bake.
children.note: Contact printing at 1:1 could reach 1 um; the Micralign (Perkin-Elmer) introduced in the mid 1970s was the cheap alternative that projected the image without touching the wafer. True 10x reduction steppers (GCA, Canon, Magnifire) were being installed in 1982-83 but were expensive.

children.name: Mask aligner: contact/proximity printing
children.description: A 1:1 mask aligner: mercury lamp or xenon source, a 20x-100x binocular microscope, a vacuum or magnetic chuck, and either hard vacuum contact (mask pressed straight down onto the resist) or a 100-500 um proximity gap. Typical 1982 units were the Coburn 2400, the Kasper 2400, the Universal Exposure Systems machines, and the Perkin-Elmer Micralign MA-2.

children.name: Oxidation and diffusion tube furnaces
children.description: Quartz or fused-silica tube furnaces, horizontal, 5-6 inch ID, with 2-4 zone radiant or resistance heating to 1100 C, a boat of silicon-carbide or quartz carrying 25-50 wafers, and gas flow panels with wet/dry mixing valves. These did the field oxide, gate oxide, poly anneal and the source/dank drives.

children.name: Polysilicon LPCVD furnace and aluminium sputterer
children.description: A second tube furnace, plumbed for silane/phosphine or dichlorosilane, for poly deposition. Aluminium went on in a separate vacuum tool: a DC magnetron sputter chamber (Balzers, Perkin-Elmer, Leybold) or a resistive evaporation chamber, both with turbomolecular pumps and a rotary fixture.

children.name: Wet etch bench and plasma etcher
children.description: Wet etches in quartz or PVDF tanks: HF for oxide, hot H3PO4 for aluminium, buffered oxide etch (HF:NH4F) for fine oxide patterning. By 1982 many fabs had added a barrel-type CF4/CF4+O2 plasma etcher (e.g. the Plasma Technologies PT etch, or an ASM) for aluminium and for poly etching.

children.name: Low-energy ion implanter
children.description: A small Van de Graaff or mass-separated implant source (High Voltage Engineering, Extrion, or Veeco) accelerating arsenic to 50-150 keV, with a beam scanning and dose measurement unit. Implantation of the source/drain had largely replaced diffusion by 1982 in a well-equipped shop.
children.note: If Norristown did not own an implanter, this step was done as an outside foundry service - plausible for a small internal fab, but undocumented.

children.name: Class 10 cleanroom bay with HEPA and FFU
children.description: Wafer processing ran in a yellow-lit room with laminar-flow fan filter units (TAMCO, Flotronics) giving class 100 (ISO 5) work area over a class 1000 background, maintained at 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases came from a bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen distribution panel with stainless steel lines and mass-flow controllers.

children.name: Bulk high-purity nitrogen and hydrogen
children.description: Liquid nitrogen trucked in and vaporised in a bulk tank; hydrogen by electrolysis of deionized water, or delivered in bulk; oxygen as a separate liquid tank. These gases flush furnaces, run LPCVD and implant hardware, and form a large part of the process cost.

children.name: Wafer probe (electrical die sort)
children.description: Before dicing, each die is probed on a wafer with a probe card: a printed-circuit board with 40 microscopic tungsten or rhenium needles, one per 6510 bond pad. A Teradyne L-120 or Fairchild SICTEST automated tester drives a test program and logs wafer coordinates, so only known-good dice go to assembly. Probe cards in 1982 were hand-drilled needle cards; automatic stepping probes were still rare.
children.note: In-process testing (wafer sort) reduced assembly cost only if the yield was high; at 6510 yields in the tens of percent, a large fraction of dies were packaged and sorted after assembly instead.

children.name: Probe card: 40 needles on a printed board
children.description: A fiberglass or ceramic substrate with a pattern of 40 gold-plated probe needles on 0.1 inch centres, hanging on a probe ring over the die and stepping down with a few grams of force. 1982 probe cards were hand-drilled or photofabricated tungsten or rhenium needles; automatic stepping probe stations (handling 200-1000 pads per die) were still a 1980s novelty for 40-pad parts.

children.name: Die separation: scribe and break, or diamond-wheel saw
children.description: The wafer is flipped onto a vacuum chuck, scored along the scribe lines with a diamond scriber or, in the more expensive method, cut with a resin-bonded diamond wheel on a saw, leaving a kerf of 50-100 um. Small dies like the 6510 (about 3.5 x 3.9 mm) were often diced by scribing and snapping, then washed dry.

children.name: Die attach to the lead frame (gold-silicon eutectic)
children.description: The die is placed circuit-side-up on a pre-plated gold lead frame pad and swept through a die bonder. The hot-tool bond (Collberg, Balzer, or Kulicke & Soffa) raises the die and frame to about 400-450 C: the gold and silicon melt together at 361 C and, on cooling, form a hard Au-Si eutectic weld roughly 25-50 um thick. This both makes the mechanical bond and gives the die a low-thermal-resistance path to the lead frame.

facts.label: Alternative
facts.value: silver-filled epoxy, or glass frit in ceramic packages

children.note: MOS Technology shipped 6510s in ceramic and in plastic packages. In ceramic (hermetic) parts the die was attached with silver brazing or a controlled glass-frit seal instead.

children.name: Gold wire wedge bonding
children.description: A wire bonder (Orthomat, K&S 1470, or Balzer 4000) pulls 25-30 um diameter gold wire from a spool through a ceramic capillary and welds it to the aluminium bond pads: a first wire from each pad to the frame (lead) and then an interconnect wire from pad to pad for internal bussing. Gold is soft, so a wedge-shaped tool presses the wire flat rather than the ultrasonic ball bond used for aluminium. A single 6510 had about 60 wires, roughly 1.5 mm of 25 um gold each.

children.name: Bonding wire from refined gold
children.description: 99.99% gold refined from ore by chlorination/electrolysis or cupellation, drawn through a die and a lubricant to 25 um. Roughly 0.3-1 m of wire per die.

children.name: Cyanide leach and activated-carbon recovery
children.description: Gold concentrate is ground to a flotation product and leached in 0.02-0.05% NaCN at pH 10.5 with lime, oxidised by air: 4 Au + 8 NaCN + 2 H2O + O2 -> 4 Na[Au(CN)2] + 4 NaOH. The pregnant solution is passed over activated carbon, which adsorbs the aurocyanide; the carbon is stripped with hot cyanide or burned and the gold cupelled to 99.99% dore, then electrolytically refined.
children.note: Wiring a computer takes a few milligrams of gold - but at 1982 C64 volumes of ~2 million machines, IC bonding alone consumed a few hundred kilograms of gold per year.

children.name: 40-pin DIP lead frame, FeNi alloy or copper
children.description: The die and its 40 leads emerge from a stamped, plated strip. Frames were made from FeNi (C4-29) alloy in a thickness of 0.15-0.20 mm by progressive die stamping on a 400-800 ton press, then plated - a nickel strike, then gold for hermetic parts, then a matte tin or tin-lead surface for plastic parts. The frame is indexed on a 0.3 inch tape through the bonder and moulder.

facts.label: Alloy
facts.value: FeNi 42/58 or C4-29, or Cu-based alloy

facts.label: Plating
facts.value: Au over Ni for ceramic; Sn or SnPb over Ni for plastic

children.name: FeNi 42/58 lead frame alloy, vacuum-induction melted
children.description: The standard low-CTE frame alloy: 42% nickel, 58% iron, with a coefficient of thermal expansion close to that of the die, so the bond survives temperature cycling. Melted in a vacuum induction furnace, cast, hot-rolled, then cold-rolled and annealed to 0.15-0.20 mm. Copper alloy (C194 with 2.3% lead) and nickel were alternatives.
places: specialty alloy strip mills, US and Japan

children.name: Electrolytic nickel from sulphide ore
children.description: Nickel is won either by the Mond carbonyl refining loop (nickel sulfide concentrates are smelted, roasted and reduced to sponge) or by high-pressure acid leach of laterite. Then electrolytically refined to 99.8% cathode in a sulfate/chloride bath and rolled.

children.name: Pentlandite (Ni,Fe)9S8 ore concentrate
children.description: The world's nickel supply came overwhelmingly from sulphide ore - Sudbury, Ontario (Inco), the Norilsk-Talnakh massif (Norilnickel) and the Philippines (SLN). Ore at ~1.5-3% Ni is concentrated to 10-30% by flotation before smelting.

children.name: Low-carbon steel from iron ore
children.description: Electric arc or basic oxygen furnace steel from hematite ore (Lake Superior Mesabi, Carajás, Itabira) plus coke and limestone, with enough residual carbon kept very low so the frame does not contaminate the wire bonds.

children.name: Transfer moulding with silica-filled epoxy
children.description: The bonded frame sits in a multi-cavity transfer press and is encapsulated in a thermosetting epoxy molding compound: phenolic novolac resin plus 60-75% crushed quartz filler, plus a small amount of silicone release agent and catalyst. Typical cycle is 150-180 C at 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes per cavity. Plaques of flash at the parting line are trimmed off in a second press operation.
children.note: Alternate route for hermetic parts: sintering an alumina ceramic DIP shell at ~850-950 C with a glass frit seal - slower, more expensive, but moisture-proof and used for military/aerospace grades.

children.name: Epoxy molding compound from phenolic resin and silica
children.description: EMC starts from phenolic resin: phenol and formaldehyde condensed with an epoxy novolac. The resin is blended with angular ground silica (fired 0.5-3 um particles) to control shrinkage and thermal expansion, mixed with glass fibre in high-temperature grades, catalysed with a phenolic accelerator, and compounded on a two-roll mill under heat. A 6510 uses on the order of 0.3-0.5 g.
places: Nitto Denko, Japan; Sumitomo Bakelite, Japan; Dexter, USA
children.note: EMC is also the material of the ABS and phenolic keyboard printed circuit boards - the same phenolic resin chemistry.

children.name: Novolac epoxy resin from phenol and epichlorohydrin
children.description: Phenol and formaldehyde condensed under acid to a novolac (phenol-formaldehyde) resin, which is then reacted with epichlorohydrin and NaOH to give the epoxy novolac that forms the backbone of molding compound. Phenol itself came from cumene process oxidation of benzene (mostly from coal tar until the 1980s) or from chlorobenzene hydrolysis.

children.name: Benzene from the coke ovens
children.description: Benzene was recovered from the light oil of the coke-oven battery that made coke for blast furnaces, and also made by catalytic reforming/dehydrogenation of naphtha. In 1982 it was overwhelmingly a coal-tar derivative - the same coke-oven coke that fed the blast furnaces and (after calcining) the silicon furnaces.

children.name: Metallurgical coke for the blast furnace
children.description: Bituminous coal crushed and charged into a battery of coke ovens, heated to 1100-1250 C in the absence of air for 15-20 hours, then pushed out as coke and quenched with water. Coke is the fuel and reductant of the blast furnace that makes the pig iron that makes the steel in the lead frame and the tin in the solder of the board.

children.name: Bituminous coal seam
children.description: A sedimentary seam mined by longwall or continuous miners. The coking-grade coals of the Appalachian basin (Clarion, Sewickley, Pittsburgh beds) were the premium feed in both the US and, exported, worldwide.

children.name: Trim, form, marking and final electrical test
children.description: After moulding, the leads are formed on a 8-16 station trim-and-form press (trimmed, bent to 0.6 inch pitch, flattened, and plated in a tin or tin-lead solder pot), the body is marked by a dot-matrix ink printer or a Nd:YAG laser with the part number, lot code and date code, and the part is inserted into a socket on a Teradyne or Fairchild automatic tester and run against a final test program.

facts.label: Test
facts.value: Teradyne / Fairchild automatic tester in a socket

children.name: Burn-in and final test
children.description: Assembled parts were run at elevated voltage (typically 7-9 V on a 5 V part) at 100-125 C for 24-168 hours in an oven loaded with sockets on a board, to weed out early-failure parts with contaminated junctions before they reached the customer. The C64 itself needed no burn-in - the chips were simply inserted into the board sockets.
children.note: Burn-in of consumer-grade MOS parts in 1982 was common but not universal; C64-era Commodore parts often skipped a formal burn-in step.

children.name: MOS Technology / CSG plant, 950 Rittenhouse Road
children.description: The place these chips were born. MOS Technology was founded in 1969 in Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, moved to 950 Rittenhouse Road in the Valley Forge Corporate Center off Trooper Road near Norristown, and was bought by Commodore Business Machines in 1976, becoming the Commodore Semiconductor Group. It was a small but complete device plant: design, mask making, wafer fabrication on 4- and 5-inch wafers, assembly and final test all under one roof, which is why a single address appears on every C64 chip marking. It closed in 1992 and the site became an EPA Superfund site from leaking underground storage tanks.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: 950 Rittenhouse Road, Valley Forge Corporate Center, Norristown PA 19401

facts.label: Founded
facts.value: 1969 by ex-General Instrument executives John Paivinen, Mort Jaffe, Don McLaughlin

facts.label: Acquired
facts.value: 1976 by Commodore Business Machines for 9.4% of Commodore equity

facts.label: Closed
facts.value: 1992, bankruptcy protection; added to the EPA Superfund NPL in 1985

children.note: There is no well-sourced 'West Hills' Commodore fab. The documented semiconductor sites are this Norristown plant and a Costa Mesa, California plant that Commodore closed around 1985; Commodore's corporate headquarters and much of its assembly were in West Chester, Pennsylvania. Treat any West Hills attribution as unverified.

children.name: Class 10 cleanroom bays with HEPA filtration
children.description: Wafer processing in yellow-lit laminar-flow bays fed by fan filter units, with a class 1000 corridor outside; 70% RH and +/-1 C. Gases distributed on stainless steel panels from bulk nitrogen, hydrogen and oxygen tanks; resist and wet chemistry in stainless or quartz benches; photomasks brought in through a pass-through hatch and never returned dirty.

children.name: Electricity for the fab
children.description: A device fab is an electricity sink, not a labour sink: 4-5 kWh per wafer per mask level for the furnaces and the aligners, plus a very large chilled-water load for the compressors and the wet benches. US industrial power in 1982 cost on the order of 5-7 cents per kWh, so electricity was a real fraction of the cost of a 6510.

facts.label: Intensity
facts.value: ~1500-3000 kWh per wafer through the whole flow

inputs: hard coal and natural gas generation
children.note: Order-of-magnitude estimate from period fab literature; the exact Norristown figure is not published.

children.name: In-house or commissioned mask shop
children.description: A device plant of this size either cut its own masks or bought them from a regional mask shop. The work involved taking the layout database to a numerically controlled pattern generator, exposing and etching 1:1 chrome-on-glass plates, inspecting them on a comparison tool, and repairing defects - a few weeks and a few thousand dollars per mask level, ten levels per part. Commodore's mask-making capability is asserted in some histories but not documented to this level.
children.note: Flagged low confidence deliberately: the existence, location and equipment of any Commodore mask shop in 1982 is not something I could verify.

children.name: Assembly and test lines in the same building
children.description: Die sort, sawing, die bonding, wire bonding, transfer moulding, trim-and-form, marking and final test all ran on the site behind the fab. The gold bonder room was kept dry and at constant humidity (roughly 40% RH) because gold wire and epoxy bonding are moisture-sensitive; the moulding presses were hydraulic, 50-100 ton, multi-cavity transfer presses.

children.name: Scribe-and-break or diamond-wheel dicing
children.description: A small die like the 6510 (roughly 3.5 x 3.9 mm) was separated either by scoring the wafer's back-side scribe lines with a diamond scriber and snapping the wafer along them, or by cutting with a resin-bonded diamond wheel leaving a 50-100 um kerf. The wafer was then washed dry, and a final microscopic inspection checked each die's edges and surface before it went to bonding - a chip on a pad would cost a whole package.

facts.label: Coolant
facts.value: deionized water or a solvent jet

children.name: Hydraulic transfer moulding press
children.description: A 50-100 ton multi-cavity transfer press with a heated upper platen, a pot and plunger that pre-form the compound pellet, and an encapsulated lead-frame strip in the cavity. Cycle: press close, 150-180 C, 700-1000 psi, 1-3 minutes dwell, then open and eject the encapsulated part still on its frame rail. A 40-pin DIP cavity set produced dozens of parts per cycle.

children.name: From layout database to mask data
children.description: The 6510 layout existed as polygons on a Calma or Computervision workstation. It was checked against the design rules, extracted to a mask database, and written to tape. A mask data preparation program merged the layout with the process layers, the alignment marks, the die boundary and a grid-broken alignment structure, and produced the flat rectangle-and-trapezoid format the pattern generator consumed. This data-reduction step - not the exposure - was where most mask errors were caught.

facts.label: Layout system
facts.value: Calma / Computervision, magnetic tape in and out

facts.label: Output
facts.value: rectangle/trapezoid tape for the pattern generator

children.note: Which CAD system the Norristown layout group used in 1982 is not documented; Calma and Computervision dominated the industry and Rohm and Haas/Shipley support was in Philadelphia.

roots.name: Four/eight 4164 64Kbit DRAMs = 64 KB RAM
roots.description: The C64's dynamic memory. The breadbin mainboard (PCB 326498-01) carries EIGHT 4164 64Kbit x 1 DRAMs, each holding 8 KB, giving 64 KB total; the address bus is multiplexed row/column through two 74LS257 multiplexers. Early prototypes used 4116 16-pin parts. The 4164 is a single-transistor single-capacitor (1T1C) dynamic cell, needs only +5 V because the 8-pin version generates its own -5 V substrate bias internally, and runs a two-level polysilicon process.

facts.label: Organisation
facts.value: 65,536 x 1 bit = 64 Kbit = 8 KB per chip

facts.label: Package
facts.value: 8-pin DIP (pin 1 no connection; pin 8 VBB on the 16-pin -8/-10 version)

facts.label: Supply
facts.value: +5 V only; internal VBB = -5 V charge pump

facts.label: Typical suppliers
facts.value: Mosel MK4564, TI TMS4464, Sanyo, UMC, Samsung, Hyundai, Nippon Micron

roots.note: The scope brief said '4x 4164 = 64 KB'. That is arithmetically wrong: 4 x 8 KB = 32 KB. A breadbin C64 has EIGHT 4164 sockets. Parts came from many Asian and US suppliers, not necessarily from Commodore's own Norristown fab.

children.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
children.description: A 4-inch boron-doped p-type CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed with a (100) primary flat. DRAM wafers were commonly grown to a heavier oxygen content (a higher oxygen precipitate density in the bulk) because the long trapped-charge lifetime helps refresh margin.

children.name: 9N electronic-grade polysilicon rod
children.description: Polysilicon grown by the Siemens process: 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated silicon filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, giving a 200 mm diameter, 1 m long polycrystalline rod that is diced into CZ charge.

children.name: Trichlorosilane purification by rectification
children.description: Metallurgical silicon + HCl at 300 C gives crude SiHCl3 plus boron and phosphorus trichlorides. Rectification in a batch or packed column on the 31.8 C boiling point takes it to 9N-11N, then it is stored in nickel or stainless bulk tanks.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%, from the arc furnace
children.description: Quartz plus petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace to give grey lumps of 98-99% silicon containing a few hundred ppm of boron.

children.name: Submerged arc furnace, 200-400 kA
children.description: Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc keeps a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

children.name: Quartz lump, 5-30 mm, under 200 ppm Al and Fe
children.description: Metallurgical-grade quartz crushed and screened from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

children.name: Quartz sand, 99.5% SiO2, mined
children.description: Washed silica sand from a high-purity quartz deposit; acid-leached with HF and HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron before being shipped to the silicon plant.

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) for the HF leach
children.description: Acid-grade fluorspar, 97%+ CaF2, mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid to make the hydrofluoric acid that leaches quartz and etches oxide.

children.name: Fluorspar vein and stock ore
children.description: Hydrothermal and karst deposits worked by open pit and underground mining, then crushed and floated. The Xe-124 emission controversy of the mid-1980s was about elemental fluorine plants, not the mine.

children.name: CZ crystal pull
children.description: Polysilicon charge melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium; a (100) seed is dipped and withdrawn at 2-4 mm/min while rotating at 0.5-2 rpm, growing a 100 mm boule 1-1.5 m long. Boron trichloride sets the resistivity.

children.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
children.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

children.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
children.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

children.name: Seed crystal and dopant gas
children.description: A (100)-oriented 100 mm seed sliver cut from a previous ingot sets orientation; boron trichloride is dosed into the melt through a bubbler to set 10-20 ohm-cm resistivity; high-purity helium flows over the melt at 20-40 l/min to sweep away boron.

children.name: Sawing, lapping, wet chemical polish, clean
children.description: OD or ID diamond saw slicing to ~0.7 mm, double-sided lapping to 300 um with colloidal silica, then wet chemical polish in hot alkaline peroxide or HNO3/HF - CMP did not exist yet. Wafers are laser-scribed for the (100) primary flat and given a rounded edge in hot KOH, then megasonically cleaned in Piranha (H2SO4:H2O2, 120 C) and RCA SC-1.
children.note: Alpha-particle soft-error protection mattered for DRAM: 4164 dice were commonly lidded with a sintered alumina or nitride ceramic 'chip cover' to absorb the alpha-particles emitted by trace radon in the packaging materials.

children.name: The 1T1C memory cell and the 4164's three polysilicon levels
children.description: Each of the 65,536 bits is one access transistor plus one capacitor. The cell uses THREE polysilicon layers: poly 1 is the word line crossing the device, poly 2 is the overlapping plate of the storage capacitor (the plate is doped n+ and shared with the bit line), poly 3 is the bit line itself. Around 3.5 um x 8 um per cell in 1982 - big compared with modern trench/stacked cells. Double-diffused poly (DDP) cells, where the source and drain are separately implanted so the cell can be offset, were used by several 64K DRAM makers.

facts.label: Storage
facts.value: charge on the capacitor, must be refreshed

children.note: The brief said '3-transistor/1-capacitor cell' - that is the 1Kbit-era cell (e.g. the 1101/2102). The 4164 is definitively 1T1C; every 4164 datasheet of the period says 'single transistor dynamic storage cells'. Folded bit lines belong to the 256K/1M generation, though a few 4164 designs did use them; treat folded bit lines here as unverified.

children.name: Second polysilicon layer: the storage capacitor
children.description: The key DRAM process problem in 1982. A second conformal polysilicon layer had to be deposited and patterned so that its edge was razor sharp and its overlap onto the access transistor was tight. Deposition was LPCVD silane at ~800-850 C; the plate was doped n+ with a phosphorus implant and annealed. Refractory metal silicides (WSi2, TiSi2) were being introduced on gates in 1983-84 but were not universal in 1982 64K DRAMs.
children.note: Difference from today: 2020s DRAM uses a sputtered AL2O3/HZO or high-k capacitor on a finFET access transistor with a deep recessed plate; none of that existed here. The capacitor area was bought by making the cell long and thin.

children.name: Single +5 V rail and the internal -5 V charge pump
children.description: The 4116 needed +5, +12, -5 and a boosted write supply, which is why it had a VBB pin and why the C64 prototype had extra regulators. The 4164 collapsed this to +5 V alone by generating the negative substrate bias on chip: an on-chip oscillator drives a capacitor, and the resulting AC is rectified to about -5 V and fed to the substrate, which also forward-biases the pn junction between the substrate and the n+ wells. Sense amplifiers bootstrap the bit line to +7-8 V during restore, and a second internal supply raises the word line above VDD.

facts.label: VBB
facts.value: -5 V, generated internally on the 8-pin -8/-12 versions

facts.label: Refresh
facts.value: 128 RAS cycles, 2 ms; RAS-only (no internal counter on most parts)

children.note: Because the 8-pin 4164 has no VBB pin, two 4164s cannot be stacked in the C128 the way 4116s were; the C64's stacked-DRAM mods all use 16-pin -10 parts.

children.name: Two-level polysilicon NMOS DRAM process
children.description: Same basic silicon-gate NMOS flow as the CPU but heavier: thicker field oxide, more polysilicon depositions (three), a heavier arsenic source/drain, a thicker aluminium (2-3 um) for the bit lines that have to survive repeated bootstrapped swings, and usually two mask levels for bit-line precharge and sense amp. Eight to ten mask levels and 100-150 process steps, versus ~50 for the CPU.

children.name: Projection printing the poly 2 and bit-line levels
children.description: The tight overlays in a 4164 (bit line over capacitor plate, poly 2 over poly 1) were what finally forced 5x reduction step-and-repeat printing rather than 1:1 contact printing, because 1:1 contact printing of a 4 um bit line over a 4 um plate feature was too lossy. Typical 1982 DRAM mask lines ran GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers, with hard-baked 2 um Shipley AZ-1354 resist and a 5x reticle on a 3x3 inch quartz plate.
children.note: Some 64K DRAMs were still made on 1:1 proximity aligners in 1981-82; by 1984 5x steppers were standard across the industry.

children.name: Alpha-particle and latch-up protection
children.description: DRAM soft errors from alpha particles emitted by radon daughters in the mould compound were a real field-failure mode in 1982. Mitigations used then: a sintered alumina or silicon-nitride chip cover potted over the die in a hermetic package; 'getter' compounds in the cavity; and softer, minimum-area bit-line and capacitor geometries to increase the stored charge margin.

facts.label: Alpha energy
facts.value: ~5-6 MeV from Rn-222 progeny in the epoxy

facts.label: Typical soft error rate
facts.value: ~1 FIT to 100 FIT per device, highly variable

children.note: The IBM/Samsung 'HAB' (hit-point-address-bypass) and soft-error work of the mid 1980s came later.

children.name: 8-pin DIP package, die attach, bond, mould, test
children.description: Dice are sawn apart, attached to an 8-pin lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, and wire bonded with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder - typically 8 frame bonds plus 8-14 internal interconnect wires for the sense amps and cell array. Encapsulated in transfer-moulded silica-filled epoxy, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, socket-tested and optionally burned in.

facts.label: Pinout
facts.value: 8-pin DIP: 1 NC, 2 DIN, 3 /WE, 4 /RAS, 5 A5, 6 A2, 7 A1, 8 VDD

children.name: Sintered chip cover over the die
children.description: On many 64K DRAMs the mould compound was not allowed near the die: instead a small alumina or silicon-nitride lid was diffusion-bonded to the lead frame cavity and the cavity then filled with a low-alpha moulding compound or left in a hermetic ceramic package. Alpha emission rate of the compound was a purchased specification in units of alphas per cm2 per hour.

children.name: 4164 photomask set
children.description: A 64K DRAM needed eight to ten mask levels: active area, n+ field, contact, poly 1 (word line), poly 2 (capacitor plate), poly 3 (bit line), the second diffusion, metal, and passivation pad - plus gate-2 test structures. The poly 2 and bit-line levels are what forced 5x step-and-repeat printing; most 4164 wafers in 1982-83 went through GCA, Canon, Magnifire or ASML 5x steppers with 3x3 inch quartz reticles, and a handful of lines were still on 1:1 proximity aligners.

children.name: 5x reticle: chrome on quartz
children.description: A 3x3 inch fused-quartz or borosilicate plate coated with 100-150 nm of sputtered chromium, exposed from a 10x or 20x artwork intermediate by a mask stepper, developed, the chrome etched in perchloric/sulfuric acid, inspected against the database on a Zeiss comparison tool, and mounted in a reticle cassette. Because quartz has a thermal expansion near zero, the reticle pattern stays put through a mask-level thermal cycle - the reason quartz beat glass once steppers became common.

children.name: Chromium sputtering target
children.description: 99.5% pure chromium, vacuum-melted and rolled into a target, sputtered with argon at 1-2 kW in a DC magnetron chamber onto a rotating plate.

children.name: Chromite (FeCr2O4) ore concentrate
children.description: Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex of South Africa, the Ural chromite deposits, or the Great Dyke of Zimbabwe - the entire industrial supply of chromium metal still traces to a handful of layered igneous intrusions.

children.name: 5x step-and-repeat aligner
children.description: An optical reduction stepper: a mercury-doped short-arc lamp, a 5x reduction lens, an x-y stage that steps the reticle across the wafer exposing one die field at a time, automatic mark-to-mark or die-to-die alignment with +-0.2 um repeatability, and a throughput of 30-60 die fields per minute. This was the tool that made 64K DRAM economics work, because one small reticle covered the whole die and one set-up covered many wafers.

children.name: Photoresist: AZ-1354 for the thick poly levels
children.description: AZ-1354, a higher-solids positive resist used where a thicker film was needed (poly 2, aluminium) so the etch could go deep without thinning the resist. Spun at 3000-5000 rpm to 2-3 um, hard baked at 120 C, exposed through the reticle at 30-50 mJ/cm2, developed in TMAH. As with the CPU, the process ends in Piranha and RCA SC-1 cleans between every step.

children.name: 8-pin DIP: lead frame, bond, mould
children.description: The 4164's assembly is the simplest IC assembly in the machine. The die goes face-up onto a gold-plated 8-pin lead frame tab with a gold-silicon eutectic bond at 400-450 C, 25 um gold wire makes eight frame bonds plus roughly a dozen internal wires for the sense-amp chain and the cell array, and the part is transfer moulded in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi. About 0.1-0.2 g of epoxy per part.

children.name: 8-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel
children.description: A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 8 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, with the bonding tab plated with a nickel strike followed by gold. Plastic-package frames get a tin or tin-lead plate over nickel so the leads solder; hermetic ceramic frames get a thicker gold plate.

children.name: 25 um gold bonding wire
children.description: 0.5-1% palladium alloyed gold wire drawn to 25 um, spooled for the wedge bonder. A 4164 uses about 0.5 m; the VIC-II and SID use more.

children.name: Gold ore and cyanide refining
children.description: Flotation concentrate leached in dilute sodium cyanide at pH 10.5, adsorbed on activated carbon, stripped and cupelled to dore, then electrolytically refined to 99.99% and drawn through a die with a phosphate lubricant.

children.name: Silica-filled epoxy molding compound
children.description: A phenolic novolac / epoxy novolac resin blended with 60-75% crushed silica filler and cured in a transfer press at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-mould-baked at 175 C. The low-alpha version used on many 4164s carried a specified alpha emission rate.

children.name: Crushed quartz filler from quartz sand
children.description: The single largest mass ingredient in the package: 60-75% by weight of angular fused or ground silica of 0.5-3 um mean size, made by firing and grinding high-purity quartz. It is there to control the shrinkage coefficient and the thermal expansion, and it is the reason a decapsulated die sits in a white ceramic-looking blob.

children.name: Wafer sort and final test of the 4164
children.description: Every die is probed with an 8-needle probe card and tested on an automated memory tester that runs a march-type pattern (write a checkerboard, read it, invert, repeat) through all 65,536 cells, then a refresh test holding 128 RAS cycles. Assembled parts go back into a socket on the same tester for a signature/AC timing check at 150 ns. Timing bins came out of this test - the C64 does not need the fastest grade, but the drive and the C128 memory expansions did.

facts.label: Testers
facts.value: Teradyne L-200, Fairchild SICTEST, or a Voltronik 5n

children.note: Specific tester models are typical of the period; the ones at Norristown or at the Asian vendors are not documented.

children.name: Photolithography for this part
children.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 4164 mask set printed on a 5x stepper, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: poly 2, bit line, metal. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1354 for the poly and aluminium levels, AZ-1350 elsewhere

children.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
children.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
children.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

children.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track

children.name: RAS-only refresh and why the C64 counts it
children.description: The 4164 has no refresh counter: the address must be presented on RAS every cycle to stay alive. That is why the KERNAL must be present for the machine to run, and why a 128-cycle-refresh 4164 (not a 256-cycle part) is mandatory.

facts.value: in the 6510's software, not on the DRAM

children.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

children.name: Mask programming: one mask set per ROM revision
children.description: An NMOS mask ROM of 1982 was an NMOS transistor array with a decoder, programmed by removing or adding contacts/metal at the array intersections. The usual 1980s implementation was contact programming: the programmer and sense-amp metal were left unconnected at a bit=1 location, and the ROM-only mask plate was drawn with those contact cuts simply omitted - or, in the opposite polarity, extra contact cuts were added for every 0. The array is arranged 32 bit lines (or 24, using 6 cells of 4 transistors) across 2048 words for the 8 KB parts.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 2048 words x 8 bits for 8 KB; 512 x 8 for 4 KB

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: contact / via programming done as an edit to one mask

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: each ROM revision = a new mask set cut and a new process run

children.note: The brief describes programming as 'final-metal selective etch'. That is right in spirit - the pattern is defined by which bits of metal/via are present - but in 1982 the edit was usually made at the contact-cut level or in the aluminium layer itself, not by selectively etching an already-deposited blanket metal film. Either way the cost was the same: one extra mask.

children.name: Thin-film alternatives: NiCr and Cr-SiO2
children.description: Some mask ROMs and PROMs of the era used a vacuum-deposited thin film as the memory element instead of a transistor array: nichrome (Ni80/Cr20) or chromium-silicon monoxide cermet resistor film, sputtered or co-evaporated to a sheet resistance of 25-200 ohm/sq, then laser- or sand-blast-programmed by burning gaps in the film. Commodore's ROMs were the ordinary transistor-array type; thin-film PROMs were more at home in TTL/PROM logic parts.

facts.value: pulsed laser ablation or sandblast through a photoresist mask

children.note: Included to record that 'mask ROM' and 'thin-film PROM' were two different ways to build a read-only store in the same decade.

A 24-pin DIP ROM die is small (a few mm2) and yields well; the constraint was mask cost, not yield.

children.name: 24-pin DIP lead frame, gold over nickel
children.description: A stamped strip of 0.15-0.20 mm FeNi (C4-29) or copper alloy, 24 leads at 0.6 inch pitch, bonding tab plated nickel-then-gold, leads later tin-plated for soldering.

children.name: 25 um gold wire wedge bonding
children.description: About 24 pad-to-frame bonds plus a few internal wires, made on a wedge bonder because gold is soft; the wedge tool presses the wire flat. Ultrasonic energy and 300-400 C tool temperature.

children.name: Epoxy molding compound and quartz filler
children.description: Phenolic/epoxy novolac resin with 60-75% ground silica, transfer moulded at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi for 1-3 minutes, then post-baked at 175 C.

children.name: Fused and ground silica from quartz sand
children.description: The 0.5-3 um angular silica that fills 60-75% of the moulding compound by weight, produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz.

children.name: Verifying every ROM bit

children.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. children.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

children.name: NMOS hybrid process: digital counters on an analogue poly
children.description: The 6581 was not a purely digital NMOS part. Its 24-bit phase accumulators, the noise LFSR and the envelope generators are ordinary silicon-gate NMOS with depletion loads, the same technology as the 6510. Its DACs, the filter and the VCA are analogue: long polysilicon resistors laid down in the same polysilicon deposition, a large-area common-emitter output transistor, and a big p-diffused 'pump' resistor in the VCA. All of it in one 2-4 um process with a single aluminium layer, and with the analogue section laid out shielded inside its own p-epitaxial tub.

facts.label: DAC
facts.value: R-2R style, built from polysilicon resistors and n+ lands

facts.label: Isolation
facts.value: p-type epitaxial tub around the analogue block

children.note: The poly-resistor DAC and the tub isolation are standard period NMOS-analogue practice (Hitachi, Toshiba, Signetics used exactly this) but the internal details of the Norristown 6580/6581 are not public.

children.name: Polysilicon load resistors
children.description: The 6510 and the SID both use undoped or lightly doped deposited polysilicon as a resistor, deposited in the same LPCVD silane step as the gate and left unetched between two aluminium contacts. Sheet resistance was 30-100 ohm/sq in 1982 and the resistance was trimmed, if at all, by laser or by anodising the surface - the 'thin-film resistor' trimming industry existed for exactly this.

facts.label: Tempco
facts.value: ~+0.1 to +0.3 %/C - poor by modern thin-film standards

children.note: Silicon-barrier anodes, nitride barriers and copper lines did not exist; a 1982 IC resistor could drift several hundred ppm per year with humidity.

children.name: Probe test with audio characterisation
children.description: Wafer sort for the SID was as much a listening test as an electrical one: patterns stepped through the DACs and the filter and the DC output measured and sometimes listened to through a monitor speaker in the test head. Threshold voltages for the envelope generators and the VCA had to be trended, because the whole reason the 8580 sounds different is that its analogue section was redesigned and its thresholds tightened.

children.name: External components the SID needs from the board
children.description: The 6581 does not make sound by itself. The C64 mainboard provides the 11 MHz colour clock derived from the VIC-II, two 4066 CMOS bilateral switches and a 7406 hex inverter to control filter routing and to stabilize the output (a documented MOS workaround that varies with chip revision), the 470 ohm/1 kohm output network, and the 4066-switched external-to-internal feedback path. children.note: The 'chip-dependent' volume crackle and distortion of the 6581 was a consequence of this external network plus the internal filter threshold, which is why later revisions changed the on-board values.

children.name: 40-pin DIP assembly
children.description: Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame with gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, wire bonding with 25 um gold on a wedge bonder (roughly 40 pad bonds plus internal wiring for the analogue block), transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C / 700-1000 psi, lead forming to 0.6 inch pitch, marking and socket test. children.note: Mould compound shrinkage over a die this large is why the SID's epoxy dome is visibly bulged and why humidity noise tracks with temperature.

children.description: 99.5% chromium, vacuum-melted, rolled and DC-magnetron sputtered with argon onto a rotating glass or quartz plate, giving a 5-8% transmission absorber at 100-150 nm.

children.name: Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate
children.description: Chromite mined from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to chromium metal.

children.name: Coburn 2400 contact printer / Micralign
children.description: 1:1 mask printing: hard vacuum contact, or the Micralign's 100-500 um proximity gap which projected the image with a 5x optical system and so never touched the resist - the technology that removed the 'mask lifts off the wafer' failure mode that plagued pure contact printing.

children.name: Gold flotation concentrate
children.description: Sulphide gold ore crushed, ground and floated; the concentrate is then cyanide leached, carbon-adsorbed, stripped and cupelled.

children.name: Wafer probe and audio test of the 6581
children.description: Probe testing a SID meant electrical tests (register access, oscillator counters, envelope thresholds, DAC linearity, filter self-oscillation) plus, on the better lines, a functional audio test: a short score stepped through the chip and the output listened to or measured on a spectrum analyser. children.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact or Micralign proximity aligner, expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. facts.value: AZ-1350 for the levels, AZ-1354 where the film must stand up to a deep etch

children.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
children.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.

children.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
children.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. children.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace.
