facts.value: ZnO disc, typically 275 V AC rated

roots.note: Placement notes: the 1N4001 rectifiers and the 2N3055/2N3792 sit in the PSU, not on the logic mainboard - the power subsystem is another agent's tree. The exact transistors and diodes on a given C64 PCB revision vary; treat the list as representative rather than a BOM.

children.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the discrete plant
children.description: A 4-inch p-type CZ wafer, 10-40 ohm-cm, mirror polished and laser-scribed. Bipolar discrete fabs used p-type CZ with a heavy oxygen content and generally a (100) or (111) orientation; many discrete lines of the era ran 75 mm wafers because they did not need fine geometry.

children.name: 9N polysilicon (same silicon, different plant)
children.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by the Siemens process from 9N trichlorosilane reduced over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C. Discrete makers bought the same electronic-grade silicon as logic fabs, usually from a merchant supplier.

children.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
children.description: Metallurgical silicon plus dry HCl at 300 C, fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until B and P are below 1 ppb.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
children.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

children.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
children.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

children.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
children.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated to remove boron.

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
children.description: 97%+ acid-grade fluorspar mined and flotation-beneficiated, reacted with sulfuric acid at 200-250 C to make the hydrofluoric acid used for the leach and for etching oxide.

children.name: Fluorspar vein deposit
children.description: CaF2 vein and stock deposits mined by open pit and underground methods, crushed and floated to acid grade.

children.name: CZ pull, saw, lap, polish, clean
children.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium or argon, pulled on a (100) or (111) seed, boron doped to 10-40 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID saw sliced, double-side lapped, wet-chemically polished, KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1. Discretes also went through a gettered or radiation-damage anneal to kill the silicon-germanium centres that degrade current gain.

children.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
children.description: The puller melts its charge in a thick-walled transparent silica cup 100-160 mm inside diameter, with several kilos of molten silicon at 1420 C and the melt surface dipping into it. The crucible is grown from high-purity quartz sand by flame-fusion around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed to relieve stress, then glazed inside and out; it is scrapped after a handful of pulls because the silica picks up silicon carbide and oxygen.

children.name: Quartz sand for the crucible glass
children.description: Acid-leached high-purity quartz sand, hydrofluoric-acid washed to remove aluminium and iron, melted around a graphite mandrel and annealed.

children.note: The gettering anneal (in hydrogen at 1000-1100 C, or in nitrogen with a CVL nitriding cycle) was what made bipolar discrete beta usable; without it a 2N3904's hFE would be a fraction of spec.

children.name: Planar epitaxial small-signal BJT process
children.description: The 2N3904, 2N3906 and 2N4124 are all the same architecture, differentiated by polarity and voltage rating: a p-type substrate, a heavily arsenic- or phosphorus-doped n+ subcollector, then a 1-3 um epitaxial n collector layer grown in an ATCP radiant-heated reactor at ~1150-1250 C with AsH3 or PH3 in H2. Isolation diffusions of boron create the tub, then the base (boron, ~0.5-1 um deep) and finally the emitter (arsenic or phosphorus, heavily overdoped to a low base resistance) through separate photolithography steps. Aluminium metallization is deposited by evaporation, alloyed at 400 C to make ohmic contacts, then the wafer is probed.

facts.label: Emitter
facts.value: arsenic or phosphorus, ~97% of emitter area (GEOR)

facts.label: 2N3904 rating
facts.value: 40 V VCEO, 200 mA Ic, 625 mW Pd

facts.label: 2N3906 rating
facts.value: complementary PNP, 40 V, 200 mA, ~250 MHz fT

children.note: Motorola registered the 2N3904/2N3906 in the mid-1960s as a pair, which is why almost every 1982 household electronics catalog lists them as Motorola parts even when another firm made them.

children.name: TO-92 epoxy mould package
children.description: Discretes were diced, attached to the tab of a stamped lead frame, wire bonded or solder dipped, and transfer moulded in a black epoxy (a filled phenolic or epoxy compound loaded with carbon black for colour) with the leads formed to a 0.25 inch pitch. The 2N3904's die is under 1 square mm; the package volume is almost all mould compound.
children.note: Difference from today: no 0402/0603 SMD package was on a 1982 C64 mainboard - all the discretes were radial-leaded through-hole parts.

children.name: High-voltage power BJTs (2N3055, 2N3792)
children.description: The 2N3055 is a 15 A, 200-300 V NPN power transistor in a TO-3 metal can or a plastic TO-220, used as the series pass element in the C64's linear 5 V power supply. The 2N3792 is a 100 V, 0.5 A NPN used in the supply's short-circuit detection, driving an SCR crowbar. Both are triple-diffused or epitaxial-base-collector designs with large dies, thick aluminium (or nickel) metallization and often a molybdenum or copper heat spreader, die-attachable with a soft solder or silver brazing.

facts.label: 2N3055
facts.value: NPN, 250 V VCEO, 15 A Ic, 200 W Pc

facts.label: 2N3792
facts.value: NPN, 100 V VCEO, 0.5 A Ic, 1 W Pc

children.note: Both are in the power supply, which is outside this subsystem's scope; listed here because they are discrete semiconductors in the machine.

children.name: Rectifier, switching and zener diodes
children.description: Three diode families with completely different construction. The 1N4001 is a diffused rectifier: an n- epitaxial layer on an n+ substrate with a heavily p-doped anode, rated 1 A / 50 V. The 1N4148 is a planar switching diode: a small npn with a Schottky-clamped base shorted to the cathode, rated 200 mA / 100 V, fast enough for 300 ns recovery. The 1N47xx is a zener: a heavily doped junction with a knee of 2.4-75 V, usually a diffused planar or, in the low-current versions, a temperature-compensated bandgap reference. All three were made by alloying or diffusing junctions into small silicon dice and moulding them in DO-35 glass or DO-41 plastic.

facts.label: 1N4148
facts.value: 200 mA, 100 V, ~4 ns; N planar switching

children.note: Older zeners were made by alloying indium or aluminium into pits cut in the wafer surface (alloy-junction), which is why they were noisy and temperature-drifty compared with the diffused ones that replaced them by the mid 1970s.

children.name: Indicator LED (red/green/amber only)
children.description: The C64's power indicator is a 3 mm or 5 mm epoxy-domed LED: a liquid-phase epitaxially grown GaP or GaAsP junction die, die-bonded into a reflector cup on the cathode post, wire bonded to the anode, and encapsulated in a semi-transparent epoxy lens that also acts as a light pipe. Red (GaAsP, ~660 nm) and green (GaP, ~555 nm) were common; amber (GaAsP ~590 nm) and the increasingly cheap GaP red were also in use. Blue LEDs did not exist in 1982 at any price - the first practical blue GaN/InGaN device was 1993, and an efficient one 1995.

children.name: Liquid-phase epitaxy of the GaP junction
children.description: A GaP or GaAsP wafer is dipped in a molten, boron-doped Ga/GaP/P solution in a horizontal tilting boat inside a long quartz tube furnace at ~850-900 C. The substrate is swept through many alternating supersaturated melts so that dozens of GaP layers a few microns thick grow in, alternating p-type (Zn-doped) and n-type (S-doped) to form the double-heterostructure junction that makes the bright 1980s LED. The process is epitaxial in the strict sense - it is the same technique used for GaAs microwave chips.

facts.label: Furnace
facts.value: quartz tube with tilting boat and zone pulls

children.note: High-purity phosphorus was produced by red-phosphorus distillation, and the gallium was refined by ion-exchange or by liquid-metal extraction - both expensive, which is why an LED cost tens of cents in 1982.

children.name: Refined gallium
children.description: Gallium refined from bauxite residue or from zinc residues by repeated ion-exchange in alkaline solution or by amalgam/hydroxide extraction, to 99.9-99.99% metal, then to GaP by reaction with high-purity phosphorus at 1000-1100 C in a sealed quartz ampoule.
children.note: Gallium is almost entirely a byproduct of bauxite refining (and of zinc), not a primary ore - this is the same trace metal that makes gallium nitride LEDs possible today.

children.name: GaP or GaAsP substrate wafer
children.description: The LPE junction layers grow on a polished, Czochralski-grown substrate of n-type or semi-insulating GaAs, or on GaP grown by the same kind of pull used for silicon. GaAs itself is made by liquid-phase or VGF growth from a melt of gallium and arsenic, with the arsenic fed from a boiler of high-purity arsenic metal in hydrogen.

facts.label: Growth
facts.value: Czochralski from a Ga/As melt near 1250 C

children.note: GaAs substrate supply was treated as a strategic material in the 1980s; Japan, the USSR and the UK were the main sources.

children.name: Zinc oxide varistor disc
children.description: A MOV disc across the mains input: a disc of ZnO powder mixed with a few percent of glass and pressed and sintered at 1000-1200 C in air. Its resistance is nonlinear - about 1 kohm/mm at low voltage, collapsing to tens of ohms at the 275 V clamping point - because the grain boundaries are thin depleted zinc-oxide grain-boundary phases that break down. Organic or glassy coating and epoxy moulding complete the disc.
places: China (the dominant ZnO supplier by the 1990s)
children.note: ZnO itself comes from zinc concentrate or from the reduction of zinc oxide; that chain belongs in the metals tree. The MOV is in the PSU, not the logic mainboard.

children.name: Zinc oxide powder from zinc concentrate
children.description: Sphalerite (ZnS) concentrate is roasted in a fluidised bed at 900-1000 C to zinc oxide, then reduced with carbon in a shaft or electrothermic furnace at 900-1100 C to zinc metal, burned back to ZnO, and purified to high-purity ZnO for the varistor mix.

children.name: Sphalerite (ZnS) ore concentrate
children.description: The world's zinc ore: a cubic sulphide mined underground or in big open pits, floated to 50-60% Zn. The Sierra de Orueba and MIDA deposits in China became dominant suppliers in exactly the period Commodore's supply chain depended on.

children.name: Black epoxy for the TO-92 shell
children.description: A discrete's package is 90% compound by mass: an epoxy or phenolic resin loaded with 60-70% silica and 0.5-2% carbon black for the black colour, injected at 150-180 C into a 3-cavity transfer tool and post-cured. A 2N3904 die is a fraction of a square millimetre inside roughly 0.1 g of this.

children.name: Silica filler from quartz sand
children.description: Ground, angular silica of 0.5-3 um mean size produced by firing and grinding high-purity quartz - the same material as the IC moulding compound filler.

children.name: Discretes lead frame: nickel, copper, tin plating
children.description: A transistor's leads are a stamped 0.25-0.30 mm strip of nickel or copper alloy, plated with tin or tin-lead so they solder into a phenolic or epoxy-moulded phenolic board. The C64 mainboard is a solder-through board, so lead-frame plating was the difference between a working assembly and a cold joint.
inputs: nickel strip or copper alloy strip

children.name: Tin and tin-lead plating bath
children.description: Tin plating of semiconductor leads was done chemically in an acid or alkaline stannate bath over a nickel underplate, later shifting to pure tin as the industry moved off lead. The tin itself comes from cassiterite (SnO2), mined in Indonesia, Malaysia and Bolivia.

children.name: Cassiterite (SnO2) concentrate
children.description: Heavy, high-density tin ore from alluvial and lode deposits; the Indonesian and Malaysian alluvial placers became the dominant supply in the 1980s and 1990s, with secondary output from Bolivia's Cerro Rico and Cornwall's abandoned tinfields.

children.name: Probe, gain binning and final test of the discretes
children.description: Discretes are probed on the wafer with a 3- or 10-needle card, then tested after packaging on a curve tracer or a dedicated bin tester. Bipolar small-signal parts are binned by hFE and by VCEO - the 2N3904's hFE spread runs roughly 100-300 - so a given lot is graded, and the C64's assembly only ever saw parts within the standard bin. Rectifiers are tested for reverse leakage and forward drop at rated current.

children.name: Photolithography for this part
children.description: Every layer is defined the same way: coat the wafer with positive photoresist on a spin coater to about 1 um, soft bake at 90-100 C, align to the mask on a 1:1 contact printer in the discrete plant (diffusion and epitaxial masks), expose, spray-develop in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard bake, strip and clean. Levels for this part: epitaxial n-layer, tub isolation, base window, emitter window, metallization. Between every one of them the wafer went through a megasonic clean, a Piranha and an RCA SC-1, because a single 0.5 um particle on 2 um geometry killed the die.

facts.label: Resist
facts.value: AZ-1350 with a hard bake, coated and developed in a bench coater/developer track

children.name: Positive photoresist chemistry
children.description: A phenolic novolac resin carrying a photoactive quinone-diazoide group. UV light converts the diazoide into a carboxylic acid that dissolves the exposed film in developer, so the image is the unexposed resist. Shipped as a 20-25% solution in cellosolve acetate and gamma-butyrolactone, spun, baked at 90-120 C.
children.note: The same resist chemistry, in a thick-film form, is the green solder-mask layer on the C64's own printed circuit board.

children.name: Spin coater and hot-plate track
children.description: A bowl coater dispensing 1-3 mL of resist onto a vacuum-chucked spinning wafer at 2000-5000 rpm, followed by a convection hot plate or IR bake at 90-120 C. By 1982 mask plates and wafers were often run on a coater-developer track that baked, exposed on a fixed dose and developed in one enclosed unit, with a dehumidified N2 purge and amber-safe lighting.

children.name: Wafer cleaning: Piranha, RCA SC-1 and megasonic
children.description: A 1982 fab cleaned more often and washed harder than a modern one, because particles - not yield models - set the pace. The sequence before a furnace step was megasonic (1.6 MHz) in deionized water, hot Piranha (3:1 H2SO4:H2O2 at 120 C) to strip organics and metals, a dilute HF dip to remove native oxide, RCA SC-1 (NH4OH:H2O2:H2O) or SC-2 (HCl:H2O2:H2O), and a megasonic rinse with particle-count filtration and an N2 blow-off. About 2,000-3,000 litres of 10-18 Mohm-cm water per die across the whole flow.
children.note: Difference from today: 1980s practice leaned on wet chemistry and megasonics rather than on single-wafer wet cleans with megasonic megasonics-in-a-cassette, and hydrogen peroxide was routinely kept hot enough to be a genuine hazard.

children.name: Epitaxial growth reactor for the discrete plant
children.description: After the n+ subcollector diffusion, a 1-3 um n-type epitaxial layer was grown in a radiant-heated vertical reactor: the wafers sat on a graphite susceptor inside a quartz bell jar, inductively heated to 1150-1250 C, with AsH3 or PH3 in H2 flowing over them. Epitaxy gave the collector the uniformity and the carrier concentration that a diffusion simply could not, which is what made the 2N3904's gain and its saturation voltage repeatable.

children.name: Isolation diffusion and its moat
children.description: A boron diffusion deep enough to reach the subcollector creates a p-type tub around each transistor, isolating it from its neighbours through reverse-biased pn junctions rather than an oxide. The same oxide that covers the tub is later cut away in the base and emitter windows - this is the 'planar epitaxial' process invented at Fairchild in 1959 and still the standard discrete recipe in 1982.

roots.name: U6 2114L colour RAM (1K x 4 static)
roots.description: The C64's screen colour memory at U6, decoding to $D800-$DBE7: 1024 words of 4 bits each, i.e. one colour nibble for each of the 40x25 text screen's 1000 cells. The VIC-II reads these nibbles during the visible portion of every scanline and presents them to the 4-bit colour DAC, so the memory must be fully static with no clocks and no refresh - unlike the eight 4164 DRAMs sitting next to it. Period part numbers are 2114L (MOS Technology / other MOS vendors), MM2114 (National Semiconductor) and plain 2114; the C64 BOM lists 2114L-30, the -30 being a 300 ns speed grade. 18-pin DIP, single +5 V, TTL-compatible bidirectional I/O, about 225 mW.

facts.label: Technology
facts.value: N-channel silicon gate, fully static, no clocks

roots.note: Three corrections to the brief. (1) The part holds 1024 words of 4 bits = 512 bytes, not 1 KB; '1K' refers to the word count, and it is 4 bits wide, not 8. (2) It is not CMOS - the 2114L is explicitly 'N-channel silicon-gate technology', an NMOS cross-coupled inverter latch with a resistor load, not the 6-transistor CMOS cell of later 6264/6280 SRAMs. (3) There was no standard bipolar 4-transistor 2114; the bipolar 1K x 4 memories of the era were unrelated parts (74S287/74S288 and the 74LS189 family are 1K x 1 or 256 x 4). The 'four 256 x 4 or 1K x 4 banks sharing address pins' description does not match the real device: one 1024 x 4 array with ten straight address inputs A0-A9.

children.name: Why static rather than dynamic
children.description: The DRAMs beside it get a refresh cycle roughly every 2 ms because the 6510 can be held off the bus while the KERNAL's refresh routine runs. The colour RAM has no such luxury. The VIC-II fetches a colour nibble out of this chip in the middle of drawing each character cell, within a few hundred nanoseconds of the start of the scanline, from an address counter the VIC owns - there is no software window in which the chip could be taken off to rewrite it. So the cell has to hold its state indefinitely. That is the whole reason for the part: it is a static latch array, and it draws more power (225 mW) than one DRAM chip as a result.

facts.label: Access window
facts.value: a few hundred ns per cell during the visible portion of the scanline

facts.label: Refresh needed
facts.value: none - 'All internal circuits are fully static'

facts.label: Power penalty
facts.value: ~225 mW typ vs ~135 mW for a 4164

children.note: The VIC-II gives about 63 cycles per character cell at 1.02 MHz, roughly 60-70 us of total screen refresh per frame, and it reads one nibble per cell during the ~500 ns the cell is on screen.

children.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer
children.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed - the same substrate specification as the CPU and CIAs, and very possibly from the same lots, since a static RAM and a CPU need no exotic process.

children.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
children.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor, cut into CZ charge pieces.

children.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
children.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
children.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

children.name: Submerged arc furnace
children.description: Three graphite electrodes lowered into a quartz-and-coke charge inside a refractory shell; the arc holds a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C and metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

children.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
children.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

children.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
children.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, hot-leached in HF/HNO3 to strip surface aluminium and iron and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to remove boron. Also the source of the silica that goes into the package's epoxy and into the crystal puller's crucibles.

children.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
children.description: Quartz destined for the Siemens reactor or the crucible is acid-leached in mixed HF/HNO3 at 80-120 C and chlorinated at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to strip boron, phosphorus, arsenic and alkali metals. Yield of semiconductor-grade quartz from ordinary mine sand is a few percent.

children.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
children.description: Finely ground acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead or cast-iron retort at 200-250 C: CaF2 + H2SO4 -> CaSO4 + 2 HF. The same HF that leached the quartz later etched every thermal oxide in the process.

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
children.description: Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity, mined from hydrothermal veins and karst deposits and flotation-beneficiated. Large deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa. Without it there is no HF, and therefore no oxide etching and no semiconductor-grade quartz anywhere in this tree.

children.name: CZ pull and wafer finishing
children.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped to 10-20 ohm-cm. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced to 0.7 mm, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (CMP did not exist in 1982), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

children.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
children.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup, 100-160 mm inside diameter, holding the melt at 1420 C. Flame-fused around a rotating graphite mandrel from acid-leached quartz sand at ~2000 C, annealed, glazed inside and out, and scrapped after a handful of pulls.

children.name: The six-transistor NMOS static cell
children.description: Each of the 1024 nibbles is six transistors: two cross-coupled NMOS inverters forming a bistable latch, plus two NMOS pass transistors that connect the latch to the bit line when the address decoder enables that column. Because it is NMOS, each 'inverter' of the latch is a pull-down transistor in series with a load - which is where the load scheme matters. The latch holds its state for as long as power is applied, with no refresh and no clock, and has to keep roughly 2 V of noise margin at 5 V supply despite sharing a die and a substrate with 1024 other cells that all switch at once.
children.note: The 'six transistors per bit in a typical static RAM' figure is a standard period statement for NMOS SRAM; the cell topology is the classic two-cross-coupled-inverter latch plus two access transistors. Cell layout (single-ended bit line vs differential, and whether the sense amplifier was a shared latch) is not published for the 2114 and is not claimed here.

children.name: The load device: polysilicon resistor or depletion transistor
children.description: This is the real difference between a 2114 and a CMOS SRAM, and it is an extra process step. A ratioed NMOS latch needs something in series with the pull-down transistor to act as a load: on 1982 parts this was typically an undoped or lightly doped polysilicon resistor deposited in the same LPCVD step as the gate, or a depletion-mode NMOS transistor (gate tied to source, threshold deliberately shifted negative by an extra implant) acting as a current source. The depletion option needed one more implant than the resistor option. I could not establish which the C64's 2114 used.

facts.label: Option A
facts.value: undoped polysilicon resistor, 30-100 ohm/sq, no extra mask

facts.label: Option B
facts.value: depletion-mode NMOS load, one extra implant

children.note: Both were standard period practice and the two are visually distinguishable on a die. The specific load device on a 2114L from 1982 is not documented in any source I could find. Lithium-doped polysilicon was used in some early NMOS logic but I found no evidence it was used here.

children.name: Pass transistors and the two-decoder structure
children.description: A 1024 x 4 array is decoded as a 32 x 32 matrix: a six-to-64 row decoder from A0-A5 and a five-to-32 column decoder from A6-A9, each a NAND-type NMOS decoder built from series pull-down strings. Each cell therefore needs two access transistors, one gated by a row line and one by a column line. The decoders are the only clocked-looking part of the chip, but they are combinational - there is no clock input pin at all, which is exactly what makes it static.

facts.label: Array
facts.value: 32 rows x 32 columns x 4 bit planes

children.note: A 32 x 32 organisation with two decoders is the natural way to build 1024 x 4 and is what other period 1K x 4 SRAMs used; I have not seen a published die shot of the 2114 to confirm the split.

children.name: NMOS silicon-gate front end for the 2114
children.description: An NMOS process in the same family as the CPU: n+ source/dank diffusion, LOCOS field oxide grown in dry O2 then wet H2/O2 at 1000-1050 C, LPCVD polysilicon gate from silane at 800-850 C, self-aligned arsenic source/drain implant with a 1000-1100 C anneal, contact cuts, and 1-2 um aluminium with 0.5-1% Si sputtered and etched in hot phosphoric acid, then PSG/nitride passivation. About 2-4 um minimum feature - a static RAM has no tight-pitch sense-amplifier chain to shrink, so it could run a coarser, older, cheaper process than the 6510.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: single 1-2 um aluminium layer, no TiW barrier

children.note: The brief suggested '~3-5 um, p-well/n-well, LOCOS, polysilicon gate, aluminium, lithium-aluminium or polysilicon depletion load'. LOCOS, polysilicon gate and single-level aluminium are certainly right. There is no p-well or n-well in an NMOS process of this era - the wells came with CMOS a few years later - and I have deliberately made no claim about a specific line width for a 2114, because none of the available sources publish one.

children.name: Photolithography for the 2114
children.description: AZ-1350 positive resist spun to about 1 um, soft baked at 90-100 C, aligned on a 1:1 Coburn contact printer or a Perkin-Elmer Micralign proximity aligner through a 5x7 inch chrome-on-glass plate, developed in 5-10% tetramethylammonium hydroxide, hard baked, stripped in hot sulfuric acid and megasonically cleaned before the next step.

children.name: The 2114 mask set
children.description: Eight or nine 1:1 levels: n+ field, LOCOS active area, contact, polysilicon (gate and, if used, the load resistor pattern), self-aligned diffusion, metal, passivation pad, and alignment/test levels, printed from chrome-on-glass plates with grid-broken alignment.

children.name: Chromite ore behind the mask absorber
children.description: The chrome on every photomask in this tree starts as chromite (FeCr2O4) ore from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

children.name: How the VIC-II reads it during raster
children.description: The VIC-II owns an internal video address counter that runs ahead of the beam. For each character cell in the visible portion of a scanline it drives the ten colour-RAM address lines and /CS low, and the chip returns the 4-bit colour on D0-D3 within about 300 ns; those four bits go straight to the 6-bit-per-channel RGB DAC and out through the 18-resistor palette on the mainboard. When the VIC releases the bus, the 6510 can access the same memory as ordinary RAM at $D800. That single-ended, mid-scanline, few-hundred-nanosecond read is the electrical reason the part had to be a static latch array with roughly 2 V of noise margin.

facts.label: Data path
facts.value: 4 bits direct to the VIC-II DAC, bypassing the 6510 data bus

children.note: The VIC-II steals these cycles with AEC low; the CPU sees the colour RAM through $D800 only when the VIC is not driving the bus.

children.name: 18-pin DIP package: frame, bond, mould, test
children.description: Die attach on a gold-plated 18-pin lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 18 pad bonds plus a handful of internal wires on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C and 700-1000 psi, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch, marked, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

children.name: Probe, sort and final test
children.description: Probed on the wafer with an 18-needle probe card running an address/data checker over all 4096 bits in a marching pattern, then retested after moulding. Because the part has no refresh, its main failure modes are stuck cells from particles and defective decoders, both of which a walking-one/walking-zero pattern catches quickly - which is why the C64's most common colour-RAM symptom, a garbled or shifting character colour, is a die or socket fault rather than a marginal-timing one.
children.note: Tester models and exact patterns at Norristown are not documented; the description is the standard period approach to static RAM.

roots.name: U17 PLA 906114-01 (mask-programmed NMOS)
roots.description: The C64's Programmable Logic Array at U17: it decodes the 6510's address lines and generates the chip-select and bank-switching strobes for every other chip on the board - RAM, ROMs, VIC-II, SID, CIAs, VIA, colour RAM - which makes it the single point of failure for the whole machine. Commodore part number 906114-01, alternate designation MOS 8700-001, die marked MOS 7700R1 / 8700R2. It is a mask-programmed NMOS clone of the Signetics 82S100 bipolar array, in a 28-pin 600 mil epoxy DIP, and it is by far the most failure-prone and most counterfeited part in the machine.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: 16 inputs, 8 tri-state push-pull outputs, 1 output enable

facts.label: Programming
facts.value: MASK programmed at wafer stage - not user-programmable

facts.label: VOH
facts.value: ~3.7-3.8 V (vs 4.2 V for the bipolar Signetics 82S100)

roots.note: Correction to the brief: the part is a 28-pin DIP, not 14 or 16 pin. The 28-pin package is confirmed both by the 'C64 PLA Dissected' reverse-engineering report and by the MOS Technology products list. Also note that early C64s used a bipolar Signetics 82S100 (or Fairchild 93459 clone); the NMOS 906114-01 came later and became the standard part.

children.name: What a PLA physically is
children.description: Two arrays of transistors and a set of 'links'. The fixed AND array is a matrix of diode or transistor junctions arranged so that each row implements one product term - every possible AND of a subset of the 16 inputs. The programmable OR array adds up to eight of those product terms per output. Each product-term-to-output connection is a physical link in that array, and 'programming' the part simply means deciding which links exist. Commodore's version is pure combinational logic with no registered terms, which is why it is fast enough to sit directly on the 6510's address bus and settle inside a 6510 cycle.

facts.label: OR array
facts.value: 8 outputs, each an OR of product terms

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: 16, of the 6510's address and control lines

children.note: The 'FE/NE' pin on this package is used for programming field-programmable variants of the device and is left unconnected internally in the mask-programmed 906114-01 - a detail decapping shows.

children.name: Three ways to make a programmable array, 1982-84
children.description: A PLD or PLA is defined by how its links are made. (a) Mask-programmed: the links are decided in a photolithography mask and are present or absent as fabricated silicon; cheapest per unit at volume, but needs a unique mask set, a long lead time and a minimum order. (b) Fusible-link: every link exists as a real wire - typically nichrome or titanium - and a programmer blows selected links with a laser or a high-current pulse. Generic catalogue parts with a wide range of functions, user-programmable in seconds. (c) Antifuse: the links start as a conducting amorphous-silicon or silicon-dioxide layer and a pulse converts the selected ones into high-resistance insulation. Commodore's 906114-01 is (a).

facts.label: (a) Mask
facts.value: one-off NRE, lowest unit cost, 3-6 week cycle, minimum order

facts.label: (b) Fusible link
facts.value: nickchrome or titanium link blown by laser, seconds per part

facts.label: (c) Antifuse
facts.value: a-Si or SiO2 link blown open by a programming pulse

children.name: Mask-programmed route (this part)
children.description: The array is fabricated complete, with the links built into one of the lithography levels. There is no programming step at all: every 906114-01 off the line is already a working C64 address decoder. The cost sits entirely up front as non-recurring engineering - artwork, mask plates, mask fabrication and verification - and it is paid once per unique logic function.

facts.label: Cycle time
facts.value: 3-6 weeks from artwork to tested parts

facts.label: Minimum order
facts.value: one wafer run's worth - tens of thousands of dice

children.name: Fusible-link route, for contrast
children.description: The 82S100 that gave the C64 PLA its name was originally marketed as a field-programmable bipolar array: its links were real chromium or nichrome fuses, and a laser programmer burned out the unwanted ones through the package's FE/NE pin. This is how the PAL 16L8 and 20L8 worked, and it is why a PAL is a catalogue part you can buy in thousands of different functions. Commodore could not use this route for a part sold in the millions at commodity logic prices, so they went to masks.

facts.label: Link material
facts.value: chromium or nichrome film, 1-3 um thick

children.note: Whether early C64 82S100 parts arrived pre-programmed from Signetics or programmed in-house is not something I could establish.

children.name: Antifuse route, for contrast
children.description: A link that starts conducting and is blown into an insulator. Fay's 1970 antifuse used a dielectric-coated metal; by 1982 the dominant versions were amorphous silicon and silicon dioxide films, written by a ~20-40 V pulse that punctured the film. Antifuses are tiny and need no laser, but they were slower to program and harder to test than blowing a metal fuse.

children.name: The fuse pattern is one more photomask
children.description: This is the practical heart of a mask-programmed PLA. The AND array, the OR array and the decoders are all routine NMOS layers, but the pattern of which links exist is frozen into a single additional mask level - drawn as one extra colour plane in the layout database and cut like any other plate. That one extra mask is what makes each unique logic function expensive: artwork generation, mask fabrication and inspection all have to be repeated, and the wafer run cannot be short because the lot must be big enough to be worth the NRE. The whole array is physically small, so a 4-inch wafer holds many thousands of dies - the constraint on order size is mask and engineering cost, not silicon.

facts.label: Revisions
facts.value: each logic change costs a whole new mask set

children.note: This is the mechanical reason the 906114-01 is unreplaceable in practice: there is no second source, no substitute function, and no way to change the logic without new silicon.

children.name: Custom chrome-on-glass plate for the C64 address map
children.description: A 1:1 chrome-on-glass or 5x quartz plate carrying the link pattern for the C64's memory map - ROM, RAM, I/O, colour RAM, cartridge and bank switching. Cut from the design database, inspected against it, defect-repaired, and stored in a mask library. One plate per unique function, like a custom printing plate.

children.name: Chromite ore for the mask absorber
children.description: Chromite (FeCr2O4) concentrate from the Bushveld Complex, the Urals or Zimbabwe's Great Dyke, smelted to ferrochrome and refined to 99.5% chromium for sputtering onto the plate.

children.name: PLA versus PAL: why the name misleads
children.description: The C64's part is called a PLA, but the parts most readers know by that name - the 16L8, 16R8, 20L8 - are PALs, and the two are not interchangeable in sourcing or programming. A PAL is a generic catalogue device: every 16L8 from every vendor is the same silicon, and the buyer programs it. A mask-programmed PLA is a custom device: the buyer cannot program it, and nobody else ever made this function. That is the whole reason fakes are so common - the SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton and PLAtinum parts sold as replacements are typically GAL/EPROM emulations or freshly mask-programmed parts from a third party, and the C64's PLA is precisely the component where a substitute can fail in ways that are hard to trace.

facts.label: PAL 16L8
facts.value: 10 inputs x 8 registered outputs, 64 x 32 fuse AND array, fusible, generic

facts.label: GAL 16V8
facts.value: fuse-programmed, EEPROM fuse link, generic catalogue part
mask programmed, one-off function, no equivalent catalogue part

children.note: Also worth knowing: the 906114 family covered several Commodore machines - 906114-01 for the C64, 906114-04 for the B256, and MOS 8721 (315012-01, 48-pin) elsewhere - but each is a different custom mask.

children.name: Reverse-engineered from a Signetics 82S100
children.description: Early C64s shipped with a bipolar Signetics 82S100, or the Fairchild 93459 clone of it; Signetics was acquired by Philips, which renamed the part PLS100. Commodore's engineers then decapped the bipolar part, photographed it with a Polaroid camera and rebuilt the function as a mask-programmed NMOS design - Bil Herd's recollection is 'We reverse engineered the PLA from Signetics using a polaroid camera'. The resulting die is marked MOS 7700R1 or 8700R2, and it runs at a slightly lower VOH than the bipolar original (about 3.7-3.8 V against 4.2 V), which is part of why early and late C64s behave marginally differently.

children.name: The economics of one custom mask set
children.description: The 906114-01 encodes the entire C64 memory map in a die smaller than the fingertip, and Commodore sold millions of C64s, so once the mask was paid for the part was dirt cheap per unit. But the flip side is that the function exists nowhere else in the world. Any machine needing a different bank-switch map needs a different mask, a different lot and a different lead time - which is why C64Cs needed a different PLA (MOS 8721) to support the cartridge port's new banking. It is also why the cost of a single counterfeit or of a dead original is disproportionate to the value of the silicon inside it.

facts.label: NRE
facts.value: artwork + mask set + verification, once per function

facts.label: Unit cost
facts.value: trivial once masked - the die is tiny and needs no exotic process

facts.label: Consequence
facts.value: single-sourced, no drop-in replacement, counterfeiting pressure

children.note: The specific dollar cost of a mask set in 1982 is not something I found; period sources put a full 8-10 level NMOS mask set in the low tens of thousands of dollars, with mask plates alone a few hundred to a couple of thousand per level.

children.name: 100 mm CZ silicon wafer for the 906114
children.description: A 4-inch p-type (100) CZ wafer, 10-20 ohm-cm, polished and laser-scribed. The NMOS PLA was made in-house at MOS Technology's Norristown plant, so this wafer almost certainly came out of the same furnace and the same process as the 6510 and the 6526 - which is the strongest evidence for the process family, even though no 906114-01 process manual has ever been published.

children.name: 9N polysilicon from the Siemens process
children.description: Polycrystalline silicon grown by reducing 9N trichlorosilane with pure hydrogen over DC-heated filaments at ~1150 C in a bell-jar reactor.

children.name: Trichlorosilane, 9N, by rectification
children.description: Metallurgical silicon chlorinated with dry HCl at 300 C, then fractionally distilled at its 31.8 C boiling point until boron and phosphorus are below 1 ppb.

children.name: Metallurgical silicon, 98-99%
children.description: Quartz and petroleum coke smelted at 1900-2200 C in a submerged arc furnace at 200-400 kA.

children.name: Submerged arc furnace
children.description: Three graphite electrodes in a refractory shell maintain a molten submerged zone at 1900-2200 C; metal is tapped every 1-2 hours.

children.name: Metallurgical-grade quartz lump
children.description: Screened 5-30 mm quartz under 200 ppm Al and Fe from a pegmatite or quartzite vein.

children.name: High-purity quartz sand, mined and leached
children.description: Washed silica sand from a quartz deposit, acid-leached in HF/HNO3 and chlorinated at 800-1000 C to strip aluminium, iron and boron.

children.name: Semiconductor-grade quartz purification
children.description: Hot HF/HNO3 leach to strip surface aluminium and iron, then chlorination at 800-1000 C in dry Cl2 with carbon to remove boron, phosphorus and arsenic. Yield from ordinary sand is a few percent.

children.name: Hydrofluoric acid from fluorspar
children.description: Acid-grade fluorspar treated with concentrated sulfuric acid in a lead retort at 200-250 C to make the HF that leached the quartz and etched the oxide.

children.name: Fluorspar (CaF2) concentrate
children.description: Acid-grade fluorspar at 97%+ purity mined from hydrothermal veins and karst and flotation-beneficiated, from deposits at San Luis Potosi in Mexico and Plettenberg Bay in South Africa.

children.name: CZ pull and wafer finishing
children.description: Polysilicon melted in a fused quartz crucible at 1420 C under flowing helium, pulled on a (100) seed at 2-4 mm/min, boron doped. Boule ground, flats laser-scribed, OD or ID diamond saw sliced, double-side lapped to 300 um, wet-chemically polished (no CMP in this period), KOH edge-rounded, megasonically cleaned in Piranha and RCA SC-1 with 10-18 Mohm-cm water.

children.name: Fused quartz CZ crucible
children.description: A thick-walled transparent silica cup flame-fused from acid-leached quartz sand around a rotating graphite mandrel at ~2000 C, annealed and glazed, then scrapped after a handful of pulls.

children.name: NMOS process for the 906114-01 (node not claimed)
children.description: The device-level facts are solid: it is NMOS, mask programmed, made at Norristown, and running a lower VOH than the bipolar original. The process details are not published anywhere. On the evidence of die markings, the era and the same fab, it is almost certainly the house silicon-gate NMOS flow used for the 6510, 6522 and 6526 - n+ diffusion, LOCOS field oxide, LPCVD polysilicon, self-aligned source/drain, contact cuts, one aluminium layer, PSG or nitride passivation - run at whatever line width that flow was at the time. I am deliberately not asserting a specific figure for that line width, because no source states one for this part.

facts.label: Metal
facts.value: aluminium; no barrier metal in this period

children.note: Explicitly low confidence and deliberately vague. The 906114-01's internal process has never been documented; inferring it from the rest of the CSG part family is an assumption, not a fact. What is not in doubt is the programming mechanism, which is the point of this branch.

children.name: 28-pin 600 mil DIP package
children.description: A wide-body package because the array needs 16 inputs, 8 outputs, an output enable, the unused FE/NE pin, VCC and VSS. Die attach on a gold-plated lead frame by gold-silicon eutectic at 400-450 C, about 28 pad bonds on a 25 um gold wedge bonder, transfer moulding in silica-filled epoxy at 150-180 C, leads formed to 0.6 inch pitch in a 28-socket trim-and-form operation, marked with the part number and date code, and socket-tested. The lead-frame, bonding-wire and moulding-compound stories are identical to the CPU's and are not repeated here.

facts.label: Ceramic variant
facts.value: exists but uncommon in a C64

children.name: Why it fails more than anything else in the machine
children.description: Three reasons stack up. First, it is a single point of failure: if any of its eight strobes misbehaves, the symptom is a dead or misbehaving machine rather than one dead chip. Second, its output enable and eight outputs switch hard on every 6510 cycle against the capacitive load of the whole board, so it is the highest-current part on the bus and the one that sees the worst ringing. Third, and decisively for longevity, it is the one chip that cannot be replaced: a dead 6510 can be bought new; a dead 906114-01 cannot, so in practice a dead PLA means a dead machine unless it is re-masked or emulated.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: 8 push-pull tri-state, switched every CPU cycle

facts.label: Replacement parts
facts.value: SuperPLA, realPLA, PLA20V8, PLAnkton, PLAtinum - all substitutes, none original

children.name: Probe, truth-table test and final test
children.description: A PLA is uniquely testable because its specification is a truth table rather than a waveform. On probe, a stored truth table is stepped through all 16 inputs x /OE combinations on all 8 outputs - a few thousand vectors - which catches a stuck link, a shorted link or a bad decoder in seconds. Assembled parts get the same vector set in a socket on an automatic tester, plus a timing check that the address decode settles inside a 6510 cycle.
children.note: Exhaustive truth-table testing of a PLA is standard period practice and is the reason PLDs had unusually high measured reliability despite being un-reworkable in the field.
